# A simple mathematical modelling study of the efficacy of contact tracing in curtailing the spread of COVID-19

Xiaoying Hu1,
Xiaomei Feng1,
Xiangkai Huang1,
Xiaofeng Wang1,
Yongjin Wang1,
Yongfeng Chen1,
Yong Hou1,
Jianhong Wu2,
Guangdi Huang1Email author and
Xiangyong Fang1Email author1, 3

https://doi.org/10.1186/s12971-020-01045-6

Accepted: 22 July 2020

Published: 30 July 2020

Abstract

## Background

Contact tracing is a core strategy for controlling the spread of infectious diseases. The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the importance of contact tracing, but there is a lack of modelling studies to guide its implementation. Here, we present a simple mathematical model to study the impact of contact tracing on the spread of COVID-19.

## Methods

We used a simple SIR model with vital dynamics and mass action incidence to represent the general transmission dynamics of COVID-19. We then extended the model to incorporate contact tracing. We studied the impact of contact tracing on the effective reproduction number and the final size of the epidemic.

## Results

Our results show that contact tracing can significantly reduce the effective reproduction number and the final size of the epidemic, even if the tracing is not perfect. The effectiveness of contact tracing depends on the tracing rate and the reduction in transmission achieved by isolating traced contacts. Our results also suggest that contact tracing is most effective when combined with other control measures, such as social distancing and mask-wearing.

## Conclusions

Contact tracing is a powerful tool for controlling the spread of COVID-19. Our simple mathematical model provides a framework for understanding the impact of contact tracing and for guiding its implementation. Further research is needed to refine our model and to study the optimal strategies for implementing contact tracing in different settings.

## Keywords

COVID-19, Contact tracing, Mathematical model, Epidemic control

Zambia is currently experiencing a second wave of SARS-CoV-2 infections. The Lusaka province has the highest number of cases and deaths. Active case finding by blanket testing of the general population is being considered as a strategy to reduce the spread of the virus. We developed a simplified deterministic susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) mathematical model to assess the effect of active isolation of SARS-CoV-2 infected but asymptomatic individuals through blanket testing for control of the outbreak in Lusaka Province of Zambia. The model was parameterized using data from the Lusaka province and the published literature. We assessed the effect of blanket testing of the general population at different intervals (14, 7, 5, 3, and 1 days) to identify cases of SARS-CoV-2 infection, isolate them, and break chains of transmission. The basic reproduction number (R0) for SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka was estimated to be 3.2 (95% CI: 2.8–3.7). Our results show that blanket testing every 14 days can identify 44% of cases, every 7 days can identify 64% of cases, every 5 days can identify 71% of cases, every 3 days can identify 78% of cases, and daily testing can identify 83% of cases. The number of cases identified increases as the interval between blanket tests decreases. However, the impact on the trajectory of the epidemic is only significant when cases are identified every 7 days or less. Active isolation of cases through blanket testing every 7 days or less can reduce the number of cases by 21% and the number of deaths by 26% during the course of the epidemic. These results suggest that blanket testing of the general population can be an effective strategy to control the spread of SARS-CoV-2. Active case finding by blanket testing of the general population every 7 days or less can reduce the spread of SARS-CoV-2 and the number of deaths during the course of the epidemic in Lusaka, Zambia. However, the benefits of blanket testing every 7 days or less may be limited to areas with a low prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 infection and a low case fatality rate. Further research is needed to determine the optimal interval for blanket testing in different settings.

Text:
Plain text:
Polygenic scores (PGS) are widely used in biomedical research, but their generalizability across populations is unclear. We show that PGS calculated in individuals of non-African ancestry have low generalizability in African populations, even when calculated in extremely large samples. We identify two major factors contributing to this low generalizability: African populations have greater genetic diversity than non-African populations, and they also have greater environmental diversity, which affects gene expression. We find that polygenic burden, a measure of the total number of risk alleles in an individual, is a better predictor of disease outcomes in African populations than PGS. Our results suggest that PGS should be calculated and used within the population of interest, and that disease risk prediction in diverse populations will require the inclusion of environmental factors that affect gene expression.

```python
                continue
            
            # Check if sentence is in the translation examples
            for example in self.translation_examples:
                if example['source'] == sentence:

                    break
            else:

        return translated_text.strip()
```

# Evaluation of Visual and Cytology Screening in Preventing Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia

## Abstract

### Background

Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in Namibia. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of visual screening (VS) and cytology screening (CS) in preventing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 and 3 (CIN2/3) and cervical cancer (CaCx).

### Methods

A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the Namibian National Cancer Registry (NNCR) and the Windhoek District Health Management Team (DHMT). The study population consisted of all women who underwent VS or CS between 2008 and 2018. The primary outcome was the incidence of CIN2/3 and CaCx. The secondary outcome was the incidence of CaCx after CIN2/3. The effectiveness of VS and CS was evaluated using hazard ratios (HR) and adjusted HR (aHR) in Cox regression models.

### Results

A total of 1,024,260 women underwent VS and 100,210 women underwent CS. The incidence of CIN2/3 was 1.2 per 1,000 women screened by VS and 0.2 per 1,000 women screened by CS. The incidence of CaCx was 0.2 per 1,000 women screened by VS and 0.02 per 1,000 women screened by CS. The incidence of CaCx after CIN2/3 was 0.04 per 1,000 women screened by VS and 0.01 per 1,000 women screened by CS. The effectiveness of VS in preventing CIN2/3 was 83% (aHR 0.17, 95% CI 0.13-0.22) and the effectiveness of CS was 78% (aHR 0.22, 95% CI 0.17-0.28). In a recent study, researchers were able to highlight how being infected with both hepatitis B (HBV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) may offer a treatment advantage over infection with only HBV.
The study, conducted by a team of researchers from the University of Hong Kong, was published in the journal EBioMedicine.
The researchers analyzed data from 1,000 patients with chronic HBV infection. They found that patients who were also infected with HIV had a lower risk of developing liver cancer than patients who were only infected with HBV.
The researchers believe that this may be due to the fact that HIV infection leads to a stronger immune response against HBV. This stronger immune response may help to prevent the development of liver cancer.
The study’s findings are still preliminary, and more research is needed to confirm them. However, the findings suggest that HIV infection may offer some protection against liver cancer in patients with chronic HBV infection.

samples.ref: Síǹkì, Cọ́pà àti Sẹ̀léníọ́mù tí ó níṣe pẹ̀lú u ìkúnlẹ̀ àìtọ́jọ́

Research output: Contribution to journalArticlepeer-review

## Abstract

Background: The etiology of preterm birth (PTB) is multifactorial, and oxidative stress is a potential contributor. Oxidative stress results from an imbalance between reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and antioxidant defenses. Oxidative stress has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, including PTB. Trace elements, such as zinc (Zn), copper (Cu), and selenium (Se), are cofactors for antioxidant enzymes. The objective of this study was to evaluate maternal plasma Zn, Cu, and Se concentrations in relation to PTB.

Methods: This was a nested case-control study within the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study. Cases (n = 89) were singleton births < 37 gestational weeks, and controls (n = 267) were singleton births at 37-41 gestational weeks. Prematurity was adjudicated by a perinatologist. Plasma Zn, Cu, and Se concentrations were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry. Conditional logistic regression was used to estimate odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for PTB.

Results: Compared to term controls, Zn concentrations were positively associated with PTB (ORper SDunit = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.09, 2.15), as were Se concentrations (ORper SDunit = 2.08, 95% CI: 1.24, 3.48). The OR for PTB increased with increasing maternal plasma Cu concentrations (ORper SDunit) as follows: 0.77 (95% CI: 0.59, 1.01), 1.44 (95% CI: 1.04, 2.00), and 1.70 (95% CI: 1.18, 2.44) for the first, second, and third tertiles, respectively, compared to the last tertile.

Conclusions: Our findings suggest that higher maternal plasma Zn and Se concentrations are associated with an increased risk of PTB, whereas the Cu association was U-shaped. Further research is needed to understand the mechanisms behind these associations.

Publication status Published

samples.ref: Ìwà Ìtọpasẹ̀-ilé, Ìṣòótọ́ sí Ààyè àti Ìjẹgàba-ààyè Ìjàpá abígbá-pẹrẹsẹ (Malacochersus tornieri) ní Kenya
samples.hyp:
Homing Behavior, Site Fidelity and Territoriality of the Pancake tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya
Journal of Herpetology
2019
This study investigated the homing behavior, site fidelity, and territoriality of the pancake tortoise, Malacochersus tornieri (Testudines: Cryptodira: Testudinidae), in Kenya. We radio-tracked 10 tortoises for 1 to 12 months. Tortoises traveled up to 1,000 m from their home range periphery in search of food and water. All tortoises returned to their home ranges after being transported 1–15 km from their home ranges, with four tortoises returning the next day and six tortoises taking 5–24 days to return. The shortest time taken to return to the home range was 5 hours and the longest was 18 days. Pancake tortoises did not mark their home ranges with dung. Instead, they returned to sites with shelter and access to water. These sites were often within 100 m of a water source. Home ranges of males and females did not overlap significantly, and home ranges of different tortoises were clearly segregated. Pancake tortoises were not territorial, as they did not defend their home ranges against conspecifics. Rather, they appeared to be site faithful, returning to sites that had previously been exploited for food and water. This study provides the first evidence of the homing behavior of pancake tortoises and has important implications for their management and conservation.

English text:
A study of Kenyan giant tortoises has revealed that the animals use the Earth’s magnetic field to help them find their way home.

The study was a collaboration between scientists from Kenya and China, and adds to our knowledge of homing behaviour in tortoises and other animals.

The researchers fitted 20 Kenyan giant tortoises with neck-mounted devices that recorded the animals’ locations and the direction of the Earth’s magnetic field as they travelled between a protected area and a local village.

The tortoises crossed a valley and passed near a small lake on their way to the village, where they were fed and their shells measured for research purposes.

The scientists found that the giant tortoises’ journeys generally followed a path that ran parallel to the north-south magnetic field lines.

The tortoises’ preferred direction of travel was 40 degrees east of north, which the researchers say is consistent with a map sense that uses the Earth’s magnetic field.

The findings are published in the journal Biology Letters.

samples.hyp:
Plasma Pharmacokinetics of High-Dose Oral versus Intravenous Rifampicin in Patients with Tuberculous Meningitis
Go to:
Abstract
Background:
The optimal dosing of antimycobacterial drugs in tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is uncertain. We determined the pharmacokinetics of high-dose oral (1000 mg every 48 h) and intravenous (500 mg every 24 h) rifampicin in patients with TBM.
Methods:
In a multicenter study in Uganda and South Africa, 16 adult patients with TBM provided 308 plasma samples over 14 days. We used noncompartmental analysis to calculate pharmacokinetic parameters.
Results:
The oral rifampicin area under the plasma concentration–time curve over 24 h (AUC0–24h) was 39.3 μg.h/mL (interquartile range [IQR], 32.8–47.7 μg.h/mL). The apparent oral clearance (CL/F) was 10.1 L/h (IQR, 7.8–13.3 L/h), the apparent volume of distribution (Vd/F) was 6.3 L/kg (IQR, 5.0–7.9 L/kg), and the absolute oral bioavailability (F) was 47.3% (IQR, 37.0–57.0%). The interindividual variability for CL/F and Vd/F was 34% and 28%, respectively. The oral CL/F was 24% higher than the intravenous CL/F of 8.2 L/h (95% confidence interval [CI], 6.6–10.1 L/h). The AUC0–24h of oral rifampicin was 26% higher than that of intravenous rifampicin (AUC0–24h, 31.3 μg.h/mL [IQR, 25.6–38.2 μg.h/mL]). The absolute bioavailability of the intravenous formulation was similar to the oral formulation (F, 94.5% [IQR, 74.6–108.6%] vs. 47.3% [IQR, 37.0–57.0%], respectively).

English text:
HIV-positive participants with tuberculous meningitis were recruited from South African hospitals and randomized to one of three rifampicin dosing groups: 600 mg once daily for 14 days, 600 mg once daily for 28 days, or 600 mg once weekly for 14 days. The primary endpoint was 26-week mortality. The trial was terminated early because the 600 mg once-daily regimen for 14 days was found to be non-inferior to the 600 mg once-daily regimen for 28 days (95% CI for the difference in mortality -7·1, 0·6%; p=0·03), and because there was a trend towards increased mortality with weekly dosing (32·9% vs 17·5% and 15·4%; p=0·08). The safety profile was similar across all three groups. These findings suggest that a shorter course of rifampicin can be used to treat tuberculous meningitis in HIV-positive individuals, which could simplify treatment and improve adherence.

The second treatment was a single 450mg dose of rifampicin, given as a liquid. The researchers say that this dose was chosen because it was thought to be equivalent to the standard treatment. The researchers also gave all the patients a single dose of liquid isoniazid (a standard treatment for TB) to make sure that any differences between the two treatments were due to the rifampicin. The patients were followed up for 12 months. The researchers did not blind the doctors and nurses who looked after the patients, or the patients, to which treatment they were given. The primary outcome measure was the proportion of patients with bacteriological failure (a measure of how well the treatment worked). The researchers also looked at side-effects and at the time it took for the rifampicin level in the blood to reach a level known to be effective against TB (a peak concentration). The study is published in the Lancet medical journal. aller
The researchers say that a single dose of rifampicin could be a simple and effective way to treat latent TB infection. They also say that it could be a useful tool in attempts to control the spread of TB. TB is a global health problem. In 2014, there were an estimated 9.6 million new cases of TB and 1.5 million deaths. Latent TB infection is common. It is estimated that one third of the world’s population is infected. However, in most people the infection remains inactive and does not cause symptoms or damage the lungs. The risk of the infection becoming active is higher in people with HIV infection. The standard treatment for latent TB infection is daily doses of the antibiotic isoniazid for 6 to 9 months. This reduces the risk of developing TB by about half. However, about 10% of people taking isoniazid develop severe liver damage, which sometimes requires hospital treatment. Isoniazid is not licensed for use in children. The treatment of latent TB infection with a single dose of rifampicin is known as rifampicin post-exposure therapy (R- PET). Studies in Africa, Asia and Russia have suggested that R-PET may reduce the risk of developing TB by between a quarter and a half. However, these studies were small and varied in the doses of rifampicin used. Also, it is not clear whether R-PET should be given to everyone, or only to those at high risk of developing TB. Soil pH is a measure of the acidity or alkalinity of soil. The pH scale ranges from 0 to 14, with 7 being neutral. Values below 7 indicate acidity, while values above 7 indicate alkalinity. Most plants grow best in slightly acidic to neutral soils (pH 6–7). Soils that are too acid or too alkaline can limit plant growth. Soils with a pH lower than 6 are considered acidic, while those with a pH higher than 7.5 are considered alkaline. Soils can become more acidic over time due to factors such as rainfall, fertilization, and the presence of certain plants. Liming materials, such as limestone, can be added to soils to raise the pH and reduce acidity. Conversely, sulfur can be added to soils to lower the pH and increase acidity. It’s important to regularly test soil pH and make adjustments as needed to ensure optimal growing conditions for plants.

A Participatory Approach to Assessing the Climate-Smartness of Agricultural Interventions
Authors
Metadata
Citation:
Abstract:
English:
Climate change is a major threat to food security and poverty reduction efforts in many developing countries. Climate-smart agriculture (CSA) is a new approach to transforming agricultural development in a way that addresses these challenges. Assessing the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions is a key step in implementing CSA. This paper presents a participatory approach to assessing the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions. The approach is based on a framework that identifies four dimensions of climate-smartness: productivity, resilience, low greenhouse gas emissions, and carbon sequestration. The approach involves a series of workshops with stakeholders to identify and prioritize the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions. The paper presents the results of a case study in Malawi, where the approach was used to assess the climate-smartness of 10 agricultural interventions. The results show that the approach is effective in identifying and prioritizing the climate-smartness of agricultural interventions. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of the approach for CSA implementation and future research.

```python
Odontogenic keratocyst (OKC) is a developmental cyst with unique biological behavior. It is locally aggressive, has high recurrence rate and is believed to be a neoplasm. It can be found in the jaw bones and is the most common type of jaw cyst. OKC is a challenging lesion to manage and the treatment options available are many. The treatment of OKC is a controversial topic and there is no consensus on the best treatment modality. The aim of this article is to review the available literature and present an evidence based surgical algorithm for management of OKC.

The disease is rare, but when it occurs, it can cause a jaw cyst to grow to a large size. In some cases, the cyst can break open and fill with blood, which can be life-threatening.
The researchers, led by Dr. Youssef M. El-Zoghbi of the University of Jordan, published their results in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Pathology. They analyzed 16 studies that included 1,132 patients with OKC. The patients ranged in age from 10 to 80, with an average age of 39. Most of the patients (67%) were in their 40s or 50s. The disease was slightly more common in women than in men.
The researchers first divided the studies into two groups. One group included studies that reported that OKC was linked to a gene mutation. The other group included studies that did not report a link to gene mutation. The researchers then looked for differences between the two groups.
They found that patients in the gene mutation group were more likely to have OKC in both sides of the jaw, rather than just one side. They were also more likely to have OKC in the front of the jaw, rather than the back. In addition, patients in the gene mutation group were more likely to have OKC that was more aggressive and more likely to come back after treatment.
Based on their findings, the researchers recommended that doctors look for OKC in both sides of the jaw, especially in the front of the jaw. They also recommended that doctors consider genetic testing for patients with OKC, especially if the disease is aggressive or comes back after treatment.
Source: El-Zoghbi YM et al. Atypical odontogenic keratocyst: A systematic review and meta-analysis. J Oral Maxillofac Pathol. 2021;25:615-622.
```

Available online 10 June 2020


The emergence of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV) in 2002 and its reoccurrence in 2019 as SARS-CoV-2 (2019-nCoV) has raised concerns about the development of a safe and effective vaccine. The present study aimed to identify the potential epitopes of SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, and SARSr-CoV and to compare their physicochemical properties. The epitopes were identified using the bioinformatics tool IEDB and the binding affinity of the epitopes with the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) was predicted using the docking tool Vina. The physicochemical properties of the epitopes were analyzed using the ProSA, ERRAT, and PSIPRED tools. The results showed that the epitopes of SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV, and SARSr-CoV had a high binding affinity with the HLA and were stable in terms of their physicochemical properties. The epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 were found to be more stable than those of MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV. The epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 were also found to be more hydrophilic and less hydrophobic than those of MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV. The epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 were also found to be more positively charged than those of MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV. The epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 were also found to be more flexible than those of MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV. The epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 were also found to be more conserved than those of MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV. The epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 were also found to be more immunogenic than those of MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV. The epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 were also found to be more antigenic than those of MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV. The epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 were also found to be more allergenic than those of MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV. The epitopes of SARS-CoV-2 were also found to be more toxic than those of MERS-CoV and SARSr-CoV.

In SARS-CoV-2, the corresponding residues are 478 and 486. We investigated the role of these two residues in the recognition of the human ACE2 receptor by SARS-CoV-2. We used a panel of recombinant RBD proteins in which one or both residues were mutated into alanine. The binding of these proteins to the ACE2 receptor was assessed by surface plasmon resonance. The presence of both 478 and 486 was shown to be required for the binding of the RBD to the ACE2 receptor. The presence of 478 alone was sufficient, to a level slightly lower than that of the wild-type RBD. The presence of 486 alone did not significantly contribute to binding. These results indicate that these two residues form part of a minimal set of residues required for the recognition of the ACE2 receptor by SARS-CoV-2. They also suggest that 478 is located in a region of the RBD that is more important for binding than 486.

Introduction: COVID-19 is a new disease caused by SARS-CoV-2 virus. The aim of this study was to evaluate the prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias in patients with COVID-19.
Methods: This systematic review and meta-analysis study was performed on 11 articles published between 2020 and 2021. English text:
The study, published in the journal Heart Rhythm, looked at 100 people who had died from Covid-19 in New York and 100 who had died from other causes in the same age group. Their hearts were examined for signs of damage to the electrical system that can cause arrhythmias.
The findings showed that 55% of the Covid-19 patients had evidence of such damage compared with 16% of the other patients. The most common arrhythmia was atrial fibrillation, in which the heart’s upper chambers beat irregularly. It was found in 39% of the Covid-19 patients and 14% of the other patients.
The analysis also showed that small blood clots had formed in the heart in 49% of the Covid-19 patients and 12% of the other patients. These clots can break off and cause strokes.
The researchers suggest looking in the future at why so many patients with Covid-19 had irregular heart rhythms.

English: The purpose of this study is to determine the effect of the application of the STAD cooperative learning model on the mathematics learning outcomes of fifth-grade students at SD Negeri 366 Jalan Diponegoro, Pontianak City in the 2019/2020 academic year. The type of research used in this study is a quantitative approach with a quasi-experimental design. The population in this study were fifth-grade students at SD Negeri 366 Jalan Diponegoro, Pontianak City totaling 32 students, while the sample technique used was random sampling. The number of samples was 16 students, 8 students in the experimental class and 8 students in the control class. Data collection techniques used were test methods and documentation. The data analysis technique used in this study was the t-test. The results showed that the application of the STAD cooperative learning model had a significant effect on the mathematics learning outcomes of fifth-grade students at SD Negeri 366 Jalan Diponegoro, Pontianak City in the 2019/2020 academic year, with an average classical completeness of 74.8% in the experimental class and 51.3% in the control class.

```python
def translate_text(text):
    # Define the translation dictionary
    translation_dict = {
        "researcher": "aṣèwádìí",
        "vaccine": "abẹ́rẹ́ àjẹsára",
        "were not educated": "kò kọ́ ẹ̀kọ́",
        "could not afford": "kò lè rí owó ra"
    }

    # Split the text into words
    words = text.split()

    # Translate each word
    translated_words = []
    for word in words:
        translated_word = translation_dict.get(word, word)
        translated_words.append(translated_word)

    # Join the translated words back into a sentence
    translated_text = " ".join(translated_words)
    return translated_text

# Example usage
```

samples.hyp:
Go to:
Introduction
The terms critical illness and critical care are widely used in the medical and nursing literature. However, the terms are used in a variety of ways, and the concepts they represent are not well defined. This can lead to confusion for clinicians, researchers, educators, and policy makers. For example, a clinician in one hospital may transfer a patient to the critical care unit when their respiratory rate is less than 10 breaths per minute, while a clinician in another hospital may use a respiratory rate of 12 breaths per minute. As a result, a patient who meets the first clinician’s criteria may not meet the second clinician’s criteria and may not be eligible for transfer. This can lead to disagreements between clinicians and can result in patients not receiving the care they need. Similarly, researchers conducting a multicenter clinical trial may use different definitions of critical illness or critical care, resulting in different inclusion and exclusion criteria across study sites. This can lead to studies that are difficult to interpret and may not provide reliable estimates of treatment effects. For example, two studies of the same treatment may report different mortality rates in patients with “sepsis” because one study includes only patients with a high respiratory rate while the other includes patients with a normal respiratory rate. This can lead to confusion about which study is correct and can delay the implementation of beneficial treatments. Finally, the lack of clear definitions of critical illness and critical care can make it difficult for educators to train clinicians and for policy makers to develop and evaluate health care policies. The aim of this paper is to define the concepts of critical illness and critical care using concept analysis and to provide recommendations for their use in the medical and nursing literature.

Strengths and Limitations of the Study

The study has several strengths. First, to our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the association between pesticide exposure and Parkinson’s disease (PD) in a large cohort of US agricultural workers. Second, we used a prospective cohort study design with repeated measures of pesticide exposure over time, which is considered to be a strong study design for the evaluation of chronic diseases. Third, we used a validated, semiquantitative food frequency questionnaire to assess participants’ dietary intake. Finally, the study population included a large number of participants with long follow-up time, which increased the statistical power of the study.

The study also has several limitations. First, the study relied on self-reported pesticide exposure data, which may be subject to recall and reporting bias. However, previous studies have shown that agricultural workers are generally reliable reporters of their occupational exposures. Second, the study relied on PD diagnosis based on medical record reviews, which may have resulted in misclassification of cases and noncases. However, the use of medical record reviews is considered to be a valid method for PD diagnosis in cohort studies. Third, the study did not have data on all potential confounding factors, such as genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures, which may have influenced the association between pesticide exposure and PD. Finally, the study population was limited to agricultural workers in California, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other populations.

In conclusion, our study provides evidence of an association between pesticide exposure and PD in a large cohort of US agricultural workers. However, the study has several limitations, and further research is needed to confirm these findings and to better understand the underlying mechanisms of this association.

A genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen identifies CENPJ as a host regulator of altered microtubule organization during Plasmodium liver infection

Source: Nature Communications

The rodent malaria parasite Plasmodium uses hepatocytes as a host cell to establish a latent liver stage infection. This stage is essential for disease transmission and is a critical step in the development of an effective malaria vaccine. However, the host factors required for liver stage development remain largely unknown. Here, we performed a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen to identify human host factors required for the replication of P. berghei, a rodent malaria parasite closely related to the human malaria parasite P. falciparum. We identified 290 human host factors that are required for P. berghei replication in hepatocytes. Further functional analyses identified CENPJ, a component of the centrosome, as a host factor that promotes P. berghei replication in hepatocytes. Mechanistically, we show that CENPJ regulates the reorganization of microtubules in hepatocytes to facilitate P. berghei replication. Thus, our study provides new insights into the molecular mechanisms of liver stage development and highlights potential therapeutic targets for malaria control.

samples.hyp:
Biological Invasions as a Component of South Africa’s Global Change Research Effort
Go to article...


Biological invasions are a serious threat to the country’s biodiversity. South Africa is one of the world’s 18 megadiverse countries and home to 0.2% of the world’s land surface area, but an estimated 15% of its plant species, 9% of its animal species and 5%–10% of its fungal species. It is also one of the world’s 25 biodiversity hotspots, with 65% of its original indigenous vegetation already lost and a continuing loss of the remaining indigenous vegetation. The country is confronted with a high level of biological invasions, with the alien plant species richness rivalling that of the indigenous species. The impact of biological invasions on the country’s biodiversity is exacerbated by a high level of endemism and the restricted distribution of many taxa. Biological invasions are also a threat to agriculture, forestry, fisheries, human health and safety. Invasive species are estimated to cost the country about 0.8% of its gross domestic product. South Africa’s research on biological invasions is extensive and covers all aspects of the invasion process. The research is conducted at a number of national and international research institutions, and is to a large extent integrated into international research efforts. South Africa is a signatory to a number of international agreements and is represented on a number of international bodies dealing with biological invasions. South Africa’s research on biological invasions is well integrated into the country’s global change research effort. The country’s research on global change and biological invasions is reviewed and recommendations for future research are made.

This is surprising, given that the current biodiversity crisis is largely driven by human activities, which are in turn strongly affected by global change. A better understanding of the relative importance of drivers of global change for biodiversity is thus urgently needed to improve the effectiveness of conservation actions. Here, we present a comprehensive quantitative picture of the relative importance of drivers of global change for biodiversity, based on a systematic review of the scientific literature. We find that habitat modification, invasive species, climate change, overexploitation, pollution, and fire are the most important drivers of global change for biodiversity. The relative importance of these drivers varies strongly across taxonomic groups, regions, and ecosystems. We discuss the implications of our findings for the development of effective conservation strategies. We conclude that a comprehensive understanding of the relative importance of drivers of global change for biodiversity is essential for the development of effective conservation strategies. We call for more research on the relative importance of drivers of global change for biodiversity, and for the integration of this knowledge into conservation planning and practice.

English text:
The researchers found 11 genes that were differentially expressed in the sperm of rats exposed to BPA compared to sperm from rats that were not exposed to BPA. These genes are involved in DNA packaging, chromatin remodelling, metabolism, and cell signalling. The researchers also found that the sperm of rats exposed to BPA had a higher number of DNA strand breaks compared to sperm from rats that were not exposed to BPA. These findings suggest that BPA exposure may have negative effects on sperm quality and fertility in rats. Further research is needed to determine the long-term effects of BPA exposure on reproductive health in both rats and humans.

Abstract
Homegardens are culturally important agroforestry systems in the tropics and subtropics. In Ethiopia, homegardens are found in different agroecological zones, but their specific characteristics are poorly understood. This study was conducted to document the structure, plant species composition, and cultural uses of homegardens in the Daga Debo indigenous community in North West Ethiopia. A total of 120 households were selected using a multistage sampling technique, and data were collected using a semi-structured interview and direct observation. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and similarity indices.
The mean size of the homegardens was 50.3 m2, and the mean age of the gardens was 20.7 years. Homegardens were divided into three zones based on the proximity to the house: the inner zone (19.3 m2), the intermediate zone (21.6 m2), and the outer zone (9.4 m2). The most common management practices were thinning (95%), manuring (88.3%), and weeding (80.8%). English:
The floristic composition of homegardens in Northwest Ethiopia in general, and the Gozamin district in particular, has received little research attention. The present study was conducted to assess the floristic diversity, endemism, and conservation value of homegardens in the Gozamin district of Northwest Ethiopia. A total of 20 homegardens in the district were selected randomly, and the species composition, abundance, and diameter at breast height (DBH) of all woody species were recorded. The Shannon-Weaver index was used to calculate the diversity, Berger-Parker index for dominance, and Fisher’s alpha for species richness. The similarity of species composition among the homegardens was determined using the Jaccard similarity coefficient. The floristic diversity ranged from 16 to 61 species per garden, with a mean of 33.6 species. The highest number of species was found in the homegardens of the Gozamin town, followed by those of the Alamata and Gondar towns. The most common species were Eucalyptus camaldulensis, Ficus spp., and Acacia spp. The endemism rate was 1.5%, and the conservation value was 12.3%. The results indicate that homegardens in the Gozamin district are important reservoirs of plant diversity and have potential for conservation. However, further research is needed to assess the sustainability of these homegardens and to develop strategies for their conservation.
